title: Case Report: Pulmonary tuberculosis with pneumocystis jirovecii colonization in a non-HIV patient: a cautionary tale on interpreting mNGS results
case_text:
A 73-year-old female patient was admitted on January 22, 2024, with a 2-year history of recurrent thoracolumbar pain and fever. Two years prior, she was diagnosed with a thoracic vertebral infection at a local hospital and achieved symptom resolution after treatment with ceftoperazone/sulbactam. Six months before admission (August 2023), symptoms recurred. Chest CT revealed bilateral pulmonary inflammatory lesions, right pleural effusion, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, vascular calcifications (aorta/coronary arteries), and minor pericardial effusion (Figures 1A1,A2). Thoracic MRI demonstrated pathological fractures at T7-T8 vertebrae, bone marrow edema at T6, and degenerative thoracolumbar changes (Figure 2A). Symptoms improved following vancomycin therapy.
Three months prior (October 2023), the patient experienced post-COVID-19 exacerbation with dyspnea. Despite a 15-day course of intermittent steroids (dexamethasone 0.325 mg, oral, twice a day or methylprednisolone 4 mg, oral, twice a day) and antibiotics, symptoms persisted, culminating in acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis.
Five days before admission (January 18, 2024), bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) mNGS by Hangzhou Genetron Medical Laboratory detected: Pneumocystis jirovecii: 29,036 sequences (21.95% abundance), Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex: 2,544 sequences (1.92% abundance).
The patient was initiated on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SMZ-Co 0.48 g, oral, twice a day) and transferred to a tuberculosis specialty hospital for suspected coinfection management.
The patient has a history of hypertension treated with bisoprolol and amlodipine (5 mg, oral, once a day) and diabetes mellitus managed with insulin aspart and glargine. Pre-admission evaluations (December 30, 2023) showed: negative serum HIV antibody, serum (1, 3)-beta-D-glucan <37.5 pg./mL (negative: <70 pg./mL), Aspergillus galactomannan antigen 0.11 (negative: <0.5), and lymphocytopenia (0.38 x 109/L, January 13, 2024). A thoracic MRI (December 28, 2023, Hangzhou Hospital of TCM) revealed T7-T8 vertebral destruction with abscess (Figure 2B). On January 24, 2024, a C-arm-guided biopsy of the vertebral lesion (Figure 3A) yielded pus and hemorrhagic fluid; subsequent testing confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC)-positive, rifampicin-sensitive, and positive MTB DNA/RNA. A lung lesion biopsy (January 30, 2024; Figures 3A,B) and tissue NGS (Hangzhou ADICON Lab) detected overwhelming Mycobacterium dominance (73,211 sequences, 87.07% abundance; MTBC: 72,040, 85.68%). During hospitalization, bilateral lower limb weakness developed (right: Grade 1; left: Grade 3). On February 15, 2024, under general anesthesia, T6-T8 interbody fusion, lesion resection, and pedicle screw fixation were performed, revealing severe osteolysis, necrotic bone, and extensive granulomatous tissue in spinal canals. Necrotic debris and granulomas were excised for histopathology (Figure 4).
Following surgery, the patient was transferred to the ICU for monitoring. Postoperatively, she exhibited Grade 1 bilateral lower limb muscle strength, clear consciousness, and impaired cough reflex. Treatment included intensified anti-infective therapy, nutritional support, and physical rehabilitation. On March 3, 2024, the endotracheal tube was removed, and high-flow nasal oxygen with humidification was initiated, though expectoration remained poor. Upon family request, the patient was transferred to another facility on March 7, 2024, where a regimen of rifampicin (0.45 g/day) orally, isoniazid 0.3 g/day, linezolid, oral, twice a day, and post-dialysis amikacin (standard dosing) was continued. Subsequent pulmonary improvement was observed (Figure 3). During hospitalization, anti infection and anti tuberculosis measures were administered (Figure 5), as well as changes in relevant indicators before and after treatment (Figure 6).
BALF Metagenomic NGS Results (April 2, 2024 | Hangzhou Jieyi Medical Laboratory).
Dominant Pathogens:
Klebsiella pneumoniae: 64,274 sequences (31.40% abundance),
Klebsiella spp.: 85,291 sequences (41.65% abundance),
Elizabethkingia anophelis: 13,244 sequences (6.47% abundance).
Additional Findings:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex: 279 sequences (0.15% abundance),
Staphylococcus aureus: 487 sequences (0.24% abundance),
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: 49 sequences (0.03% abundance),
Human herpesvirus 5 (CMV): 2,799 sequences (1.38% abundance).

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: pulmonary and spinal tuberculosis
